title: The formula 'all prerequisites posited, can act and not act': first sense, simultaneity of power not power of simultaneity
source_text: XLV. Caeterum descriptio illa in qua libertas dicitur esse id per quod, positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, agens liberum potest agere, & non agere, hoc & illud agere, non eodem sensu exponitur ab omnibus Scholae Romanae Theologis. Quod ut intelligatur, notandum est verbis istis posse tribui multiplicem sensum. Et primo quidem verba illa ita possunt accipi quasi iis significaretur agens liberum posse agere & non agere simul, & eodem tempore contrarios actus exercere. Hic sensus tanquam manifeste falsus ab omnibus rejicitur. Fatentur enim omnes in agente libero simul compati non posse actum & cessationem ab actu, aut unum actum & ejus contrarium; ac proinde verbis illis aliud non significari, quam quod agens liberum simul habet potestatem ad actus contrarios, & quod simul in eo reperitur potestas agendi, & potestas quoque non agendi; quod in Scholis dicitur per hoc agenti libero tribui simultatem potentiae, non potentiam simultatis.
pass_a_gloss: However that description in which liberty is said to be that by which, all prerequisites for acting being posited, the free agent can act, and not act, do this and that, is not explained in the same sense by all the Theologians of the Roman School. That this may be understood, it must be noted that a manifold sense can be attributed to those words. And first indeed those words can be so taken as if by them it were signified that the free agent can act and not act at once, and at the same time exercise contrary acts. This sense is rejected by all as manifestly false. For all confess that in the free agent act and cessation from act, or one act and its contrary, cannot be compatible at once; and accordingly that by those words nothing else is signified, than that the free agent has at once the power to contrary acts, and that at once there is found in it the power of acting, and the power also of not acting; which in the Schools is said to mean that by this there is attributed to the free agent simultaneity of power, not power of simultaneity.
pass_b_english: The definition that calls freedom the power by which a free agent, given everything required beforehand for acting, can act and not act, do this and that, is not understood in the same way by every theologian of the Roman School. To see this, note that the words can bear several senses.
First, they could be taken to mean that the free agent can act and not act at once, performing opposite acts at the same moment. Everyone rejects this as plainly false.

All agree that in a free agent an act and the absence of that act, or an act and its opposite, cannot coexist at the same time. They therefore take the words to mean only that the free agent has at one and the same time the power for opposite acts, so that the power of acting and the power of not acting are both found in it together.
The schools express this by saying that what is ascribed to the free agent is simultaneity of power, not power of simultaneity.

lemmas.gloss: simultaneity of power, not power of simultaneity

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
